title: Third declension: vowel stems and irregular nouns

objectives.can: Parse nouns like πόλις, βασιλεύς and γένος and the irregular πατήρ, ἀνήρ, γυνή.

explanation.summary: The rest of the third declension is made of three families of nouns whose stems end in a vowel (πόλις, βασιλεύς) or in -ς that has dropped out (ἔθνος), and of a few common family words (πατήρ, μήτηρ, ἀνήρ, γυνή) that follow no single pattern. Each family has its own genitive, and the genitive is again what you should learn first.

sections.heading: Nouns in -ις: πόλις, πίστις, δύναμις
body: Nouns like πόλις, πίστις, δύναμις, κρίσις, θλῖψις, ἀνάστασις and γνῶσις are feminine. The nominative and accusative end in -ις and -ιν. Everywhere else the stem has -ε- in place of -ι-: the genitive singular is -εως (πόλεως, πίστεως), the dative singular -ει (πόλει), the nominative and accusative plural -εις (πόλεις), the genitive plural -εων (πόλεων) and the dative plural -εσι(ν) (πόλεσιν).
The genitive singular -εως is the form to recognise. A great many abstract nouns have it, and it is easy to take πίστεως for something unrelated to πίστις.

sections.heading: Nouns in -ευς: βασιλεύς and its family
body: βασιλεύς, ἀρχιερεύς, γραμματεύς and ἱερεύς are masculine. The genitive singular is -έως, the dative singular -εῖ, the accusative singular -έα, the vocative singular -εῦ (βασιλεῦ), the nominative plural -εῖς, the genitive plural -έων and the dative plural -εῦσιν. The accusative plural in the New Testament is regularly the same as the nominative: -εῖς.
Because the nominative and accusative plural are alike, only the article, the verb or the sense of the clause shows which is meant, just as with ἀδελφοί in the second declension.

sections.heading: Neuters in -ος: ἔθνος, γένος, ὄρος
body: These look like the masculine nouns of the second declension in the nominative (λόγος), but they are neuter and they belong here. The tell is the genitive: -ους (ἔθνους, ὄρους, γένους, μέρους), not -ου. The neuter nominative and accusative are alike, the plural ends in -η (ἔθνη, ὄρη, γένη) and the dative plural is -εσι(ν) (ἔθνεσιν).

Grammarians explain these forms as stems in -εσ- (ἐθνεσ-) whose σ was lost between vowels, with the vowels then running together. That is a historical explanation of why the endings look as they do; what you need for reading is the set of endings.

sections.heading: Family words and the woman
body: πατήρ, μήτηρ and θυγάτηρ have a nominative in -ήρ. In the genitive and dative singular the middle vowel is dropped (πατρός, πατρί, μητρός, θυγατρός); in the accusative and the plural it returns (πατέρα, μητέρα, πατέρες). The vocative singular is πάτερ.

ἀνήρ, 'man' as opposed to 'woman', is nominative ἀνήρ but has -δρ- in the other forms: ἀνδρός, ἀνδρί, ἄνδρα, ἄνδρες. γυνή is nominative γυνή but has -αικ- in the others: γυναικός, γυναικί, γυναῖκα, γυναῖκες. The vocative singular is γύναι.
These are best learned as whole sets: the nominative, the genitive and the accusative singular, which together show every stem.

misunderstandings: A noun in -ος is not always second declension. If its genitive is -ους and it is neuter, it belongs here: compare ὁ λόγος, τοῦ λόγου with τὸ ἔθνος, τοῦ ἔθνους.
πίστεως, πόλεως and δυνάμεως are not different words from πίστις, πόλις and δύναμις. They are the genitive singular of the same nouns.
The nominative plural of a noun in -ευς is -εῖς, which is also the accusative plural. Do not read the ending as marking only one case.

deeper.heading: Two-stem nouns
body: πατήρ, ἀνήρ and γυνή are among the oldest words of the language, and they have kept older stem alternations that most nouns have lost. That is why they do not follow one pattern: each preserves its own history. For the learner the practical lesson is that the genitive singular is always worth learning with the nominative.

examples.analysis: πόλις is nominative singular, the subject of δύναται: 'a city cannot be hidden'. ὄρους is the genitive singular of the neuter ὄρος, with the ending -ους that marks this class. It is not second declension, whose genitive would be -ου.

examples.analysis: βασιλεὺς is the nominative singular, the subject: 'where is the king?'. ὁ τεχθεὶς, 'the one who has been born', agrees with it. τῶν Ἰουδαίων, genitive plural, completes it: 'of the Jews'. The nominative singular of this class ends in -ς, and the stem has -ευ- there but -ε- in the genitive (βασιλέως).

examples.analysis: Four words of the family kind, in the accusative or dative: τὸν πατέρα and τὴν μητέρα are accusative singular, with -έρα, and γυναικί is the dative singular of γυνή, with the stem γυναικ-. σάρκα, accusative singular of σάρξ, belongs to the last lesson. Compare πατέρα with the genitive πατρός and the nominative πατήρ.
